newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB wants to cut gold requirement to boost profits.
newsitem.headline: SNB wants to cut gold requirement to boost profits.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) on Friday said it wants to cut its legally-mandated gold reserve requirement and be given more freedom to manage its currency reserves so it can improve its financial performance.

A working group with officials from the SNB and the Finance Ministry have also proposed the SNB be permitted to use gold lending and to invest in longer-dated and higher yielding debt by foreign states, banks or international organisations.

The SNB also wants permission to use derivative financial instruments, such as options and futures, to help minimise the market risks to its currency reserves, the Swiss central bank said in a statement.

The proposals for a partial revision of the National Bank Law were estimated to boost SNB's annual income by some 400 million Swiss francs and thus also raise the amount of money it transfers to federal and local Swiss governments.

The working group also proposed smoothing out the SNB's annual transfers to governments and doing away with federal taxes on the SNB because such taxes only serve to reduce the amount of money it can transfer.
The proposals stem from a working group that was created in June this year to examine the SNB's investment policy and look for ways to improve the management of its currency reserves.

Between 1991 and 1994 the SNB transferred around 605 million annually to federal and cantonal Swiss governments, but this plunged to 147 million in 1995 due to the fall in the dollar and yen, which necessitated higher writeoffs on currency reserves.

This drop in transfers was followed by criticism of the SNB's investment policy by Swiss university professor Thomas von Ungern-Sternberg, who said the SNB could make much higher returns on its assets.
The working group rejected this criticism, noting the central bank's primary obligation is for monetary and currency policy and it cannot admister its funds like a private bank.
"If the SNB were to speculate in currency markets, it would run the danger of presenting the public with losses of billions instead of anticipated profits," the working group said.

Of the SNB's total currency reserves of around 42 billion francs, some 14 billion are hedged and used to steer monetary policy. The remaining 28 billion francs are unhedged and used to intervene in currency markets in times of turbulence.
Although both types of currency reserves must be liquid, the working group said this condition could also be fulfilled if the SNB could invest in paper with maturities of two to three years.
The law currently limits the SNB's room for manoeuvre by dictating a 12-month maturity limit on its investments.
"This would increase earnings significantly, as long-term investments on average give higher yields that short-term," the group said.

Like most central banks, the SNB has a certain amount of gold in its vaults to back its currency. However, since the gold standard was scrapped in 1971, the SNB's gold reserves have not been used and the reserves are steady at around 2,600 tonnes.
The working group proposed the SNB be allowed to use gold lending facilities to improve the performance on gold reserves.

However, this could push the SNB below the mandated 40 percent reserve requirement for gold, a level the central bank is already close to breaching due to the ever-increasing amount of notes in circulation.
The working group proposed cutting the reserve requirement for gold to 25 percent from 40 percent of notes in circulation.

A total scrapping of the reserve requirement for gold is not currently possible because the Swiss constitution states bank notes must be backed by gold. The constitution, however, does not specify the extent of the gold requirement.
Whether Switzerland should totally abolish the gold reserve requirement will be discussed as part of long-standing efforts to revise the constitution.
